strategy: I validate the instance first. I check for unknown job or resource references, demands above capacity, and precedence cycles (Kahn's algorithm). If any check fails, the program returns "infeasible" with a reason. Otherwise a single code node runs a random-key **serial schedule generation scheme**: jobs are pulled from a precedence-eligible heap and each is placed at the earliest resource-feasible time, respecting release times and predecessors. Each decoded schedule is then improved by **forward-backward justification**: it is right-shifted in decreasing finish order, then left-shifted in increasing start order, and this repeats while the makespan improves. Starting points are deterministic priority rules (latest start from tail length, critical tail, earliest start, successor count, resource energy, topological order). After that, until a 0.9 s budget runs out, it mixes noisy rule sampling with perturbations of the best schedule's keys. An improved schedule is accepted only if it passes a full validity check. The search stops early if it reaches a lower bound (the larger of a release-aware critical path and a per-resource energy bound).

The pipeline first checks whether the instance is infeasible. It looks for unknown predecessor or resource names and over-capacity requirements, and finds precedence cycles with Kahn's topological sort. A feasible instance goes to an optimiser that decodes activity lists with a serial schedule-generation scheme: each job is placed at the earliest time that respects its release, its predecessors and every resource profile. Each decoded schedule is then improved by forward-backward justification (shift every job as late as possible, then as early as possible). The search starts from several priority rules (latest start time, longest tail, earliest head, most successors, work-weighted variants). It then runs an iterated local search that moves jobs within their precedence-feasible positions in the list, with occasional random restarts, for about 1.0 s. It stops early if the makespan reaches a lower bound computed from critical paths with releases and per-resource energy. A final checker confirms the best schedule meets every constraint; if it somehow does not, the code falls back to a plain topological-order schedule, which is always valid.

Checks run first and catch infeasible instances: unknown job or resource references, demands above capacity, and precedence cycles (Kahn's algorithm). A branch then either reports infeasible or runs the deterministic optimiser. The optimiser uses a serial schedule-generation scheme (SGS) that schedules jobs by priority, placing each one at the earliest time its releases, predecessors and resources allow. Starting points come from eight priority rules (latest finish, latest start, longest remaining path, earliest start, most successors, total successor duration, slack, resource work). Each start is improved by forward-backward improvement, which repeatedly reschedules right-justified on the reversed graph and then re-packs left. An iterated local search then runs for about 0.95 s: it swaps or moves jobs in the activity list, decodes, applies forward-backward improvement, accepts equal-or-better results, and restarts from biased random samples when it stalls. It stops early once it reaches a computed lower bound (critical path with release times, plus per-resource energy bounds).

Pure-code, deterministic validation followed by a time-boxed metaheuristic; no LLM is used, since speed and exactness matter. Validation flags unknown job or resource references, demands above capacity, and precedence cycles (Kahn's algorithm), and returns "infeasible" with a reason. Feasible instances are solved with a heap-based serial schedule-generation scheme that respects release times, precedence and integer-time resource profiles. The scheme is driven by priority keys from several rules (latest start, latest finish, earliest start, successor count, plus randomised variants). Each schedule is improved by forward-backward justification passes, then the best schedule is refined by mutation-based local search on its priority vector until about 0.9 s have passed or a computed lower bound (critical path with releases, resource energy) is reached. A final checker verifies the schedule, with a guaranteed-valid sequential fallback.

This is a pure-code pipeline with no LLM calls. First, `validate` detects infeasible instances: unknown job or resource references, demand above capacity, and precedence cycles found with Kahn's topological sort. It then compiles the problem into indexed arrays. Second, `solve` builds schedules with a time-indexed serial schedule-generation scheme. Each schedule is improved by iterated forward-backward justification: jobs are right-shifted in order of decreasing finish time, then left-shifted in order of increasing start time, which keeps every intermediate schedule feasible. Starting lists come from priority rules (critical-path tail, head, slack, successors, work content) and from noise-biased random sampling. The rest of the time goes to a local search over precedence-feasible activity lists (move a job within its valid window), with restarts. The search stops early once a computed lower bound is reached (critical path with release times, resource energy, and a disjunctive bound), and otherwise after a 1.0 s budget. Third, `finalize` re-checks every hard constraint before writing the output; if the check fails, it falls back to a trivially feasible sequential schedule.

The approach is a pure-code hybrid genetic algorithm over activity lists, using a serial schedule-generation scheme (SGS) and forward-backward improvement; there are no LLM calls. It first validates the instance: unknown job or resource references, demand above capacity, and precedence cycles (Kahn's algorithm, which also catches self-loops) all return "infeasible". Otherwise it computes heads (release-aware earliest starts), tails and a lower bound from the critical path and resource energy, so the search can stop early once that bound is reached. A starting population is seeded from priority rules (longest tail, earliest head, most successors, work content) plus randomized tail-biased lists. A steady-state GA then evolves the lists with precedence-preserving crossover and mutation. Every list is decoded by the serial SGS with a time-indexed resource profile and then double-justified (right-shift, then left-shift, repeated while it helps), which never worsens the makespan or breaks any constraint. The search runs until the lower bound is reached or a 0.95 s budget runs out.

Every schedule then goes through forward-backward improvement: a right-shift backward pass, then a left-shift forward pass, which never increases the makespan. The job orders come first from several priority rules (longest tail, slack, successor count, resource work), then from randomly perturbed versions of those rules. After that, a local search moves jobs within the limits their predecessors and successors allow, with restarts when it stalls. It stops early if it reaches a computed lower bound (critical path or resource energy) and has a 0.95 s timer budget. Before output, the best schedule is checked against every constraint; if that check fails, the solver uses a safe fallback schedule.

The approach has three steps. First, a deterministic validator checks for unknown job or resource references, demands that exceed capacity, and precedence cycles (using Kahn's algorithm), and returns "infeasible" with a reason. Second, a feasible instance is solved with a serial schedule generation scheme driven by random-key priorities. Each decoded schedule is improved by forward-backward double justification, which also respects release times and precedence, so every schedule it produces is valid by construction. Third, a small genetic and local search runs on the keys. It is seeded with classic priority rules (LST, LFT, EST, total successors, GRPW-like, resource work), applies uniform crossover plus Gaussian, swap and shift mutations, and feeds the justified start times back into the keys. The search stops at about 1.0 s of CPU, or earlier once it reaches a lower bound (critical path with releases, or per-resource energy).

strategy: PARADIGM: Chronological Schedule-or-Postpone branch-and-bound under limited discrepancy search. After deterministic validation (unknown references, over-capacity demands, Kahn cycle detection), the solver explores the space of active schedules directly with a constraint-programming style tree. At each node it picks the eligible job with the earliest resource-feasible start and branches between "start now" and "postpone until its earliest start changes". A dominance rule fails postponed jobs whose earliest start never moved. Nodes are pruned against the incumbent with three bounds: resource-aware heads plus critical-path tails, a per-resource energy test against UB-1, and a global critical-path and energy bound that stops the search once the incumbent is proven optimal. The number of postpone decisions on a path is limited and raised step by step (0, 1, 2, ...), so the search widens gradually and ends with an optimality proof if it finishes without a cut. A short rule-based incumbent and a sequential fallback guarantee a valid answer, and the final schedule is re-checked against every hard constraint.

The leftover time goes to the existing schedule-or-postpone branch-and-bound with limited discrepancy, seeded with the GA incumbent. DIAGNOSIS: The program finds good schedules mainly through one-pass priority rules and a short burst of random restarts (0.15 s). After that, a chronological branch-and-bound searches from scratch. Under limited discrepancy search, that tree only gets through the first few postpone decisions on 15–40-job instances before time runs out. Nothing in the program ever improves an existing schedule. There is no reordering of a good job sequence and no left/right compaction. The weak instances show this: big idle gaps sit in the middle (release_times, medium) and resource-heavy jobs are stuck at the end of the schedule. I insert a steady-state genetic algorithm over precedence-feasible activity lists before the branch-and-bound.
- Seeding: the population starts from the existing priority rules plus randomised-tail rules.
- Recombination: one-point precedence-preserving crossover plus swaps of adjacent unrelated jobs.
- Decoding: each list is turned into a schedule by the serial schedule-generation scheme (place jobs in list order at their earliest feasible time). Then double justification (forward-backward improvement) is applied in place:
  - right-shift every job as late as possible in decreasing-finish order, keeping its successors and the makespan fixed;
  - then left-shift every job as early as possible in increasing-start order, respecting release times and predecessors.
- Lamarckian update: the compacted schedule's start order is written back as the individual's list.

A deterministic validator first detects infeasible instances: unknown references, over-capacity demands and precedence cycles. A GA-plus-forward-backward node, seeded with priority rules, runs on a size-dependent budget and stores its incumbent in state. A branch-and-bound node then searches start-ordered serial schedule construction with heads+tails, resource-energy and dead-end pruning plus a table of seen partial states. On small instances this is one full search; on large ones it is repeated node-limited dives guided by a noisy copy of the incumbent. Every improved schedule is checked for validity before it replaces the output.

PARADIGM: Iterative Flattening on Partial-Order Schedules (precedence-constraint posting, in the style of Cesta/Oddi/Smith IFlat). The solver never searches start times or activity lists directly. It searches the space of extra precedence edges added to the temporal network. Each step computes the earliest-start solution of the network and finds the earliest resource peak. It then resolves that peak by posting one ordering edge between two contending jobs, chosen by least resulting path length (head + duration + tail) with controlled randomisation. Once the network is resource-feasible, a relaxation phase removes a random fraction of the posted edges that touch the critical path and re-flattens. It accepts non-worsening networks and restarts from the best one when progress stalls. Deterministic validation (unknown references, over-capacity demands, Kahn cycle detection) comes first. A serial-SGS safety net and a final independent feasibility check guarantee that every "ok" answer is valid.

The program first validates the instance deterministically and reports "infeasible" for an unknown job, an unknown resource, a demand above capacity, or a cycle. It then builds a strong incumbent quickly: priority-rule serial SGS, forward-backward justification, and a short local search. The rest of the CPU budget goes to an exact depth-first branch and bound over serial-SGS activity lists. The B&B prunes with a release-aware head+tail bound, a per-resource energy bound against the residual capacity profile, and a transposition table of partial schedules. Every candidate is checked by a hard-constraint validator before output, with a plain topological SGS schedule as fallback.
change:
DIAGNOSIS: The program only searches heuristically. It samples priority lists, decodes them with serial SGS, and applies small random list perturbations. It has no way to systematically explore the space of active schedules or prove that one is optimal. The weakest instances are small (11–15 jobs) with large gaps, such as release_times at 55, medium at 40 and tight_resources at 44. On instances that size an exact enumeration of active schedules with good pruning can often close the gap or reach the optimum. Random sampling just keeps hitting the same local optimum. The heuristic phase (priority rules, FBI and local search) stays, but it now gets only about 0.45 s. Its best schedule becomes the incumbent for a new depth-first branch and bound. The B&B branches over precedence-feasible activity lists (a precedence tree). Each eligible job is placed at its earliest resource-feasible time, and this set of schedules always contains an optimal one. Jobs with no resource use are placed immediately without branching. Each node is pruned three ways:
- **Head+tail bound:** release dates and actual earliest feasible starts are propagated to every unscheduled job, and its longest path to the end is added.
- **Energy bound:** for each resource, the remaining work must fit into the capacity still free at or after the earliest time it could start.
- **Transposition table:** a partial schedule that has already been explored is skipped.

strategy: PARADIGM: Time-Window Large-Neighbourhood Search with exact local repair (ruin-and-recreate on start-time windows). After deterministic validation (unknown job or resource, demand above capacity, Kahn cycle check), a few priority-rule schedules give a valid starting incumbent. The core loop never mutates priority lists. It freezes every job outside a randomly chosen window of consecutive jobs in start-time order. It then solves the window sub-problem exactly with a small depth-first search, against the frozen jobs' residual resource profile and with deadlines from frozen successors. The repaired schedule is compacted globally by left/right justification and accepted if it is not worse, with rare worse moves allowed. The search stops at the release-aware critical-path/energy lower bound or at the time budget, and a final checker falls back to a construction schedule that is valid by design.
